articles.title: Scientists discover the first diplodocus ever found outside North America
articles.summary: A 150-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Spain has been identified as the first confirmed Diplodocus ever found outside North America. The giant sauropod measured about 25 meters long and was preserved well enough for researchers to match distinctive features in its tail bones to the famous genus. Its unexpected appearance in Europe suggests dinosaurs were moving between the continents during the Late Jurassic, possibly across temporary land connections.
articles.content:
Paleontologists have identified the first known evidence of Diplodocus outside North America, a discovery that changes scientists' understanding of where the iconic dinosaur lived during the Late Jurassic.

The sauropod fossils were described by researchers from the Fundación Conjunto Paleontológico de Teruel-Dinópolis in the peer-reviewed Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. The specimen is also among the most complete diplodocid skeletons ever uncovered in Europe.

First Diplodocus Found in Europe

The fossils were discovered at the La Tejería site in El Castellar, Teruel, Spain. During excavations, a team of paleontologists from the Fundación Dinópolis recovered 14 exceptionally well-preserved caudal (tail) vertebrae along with several chevron bones.

Before this discovery, every confirmed Diplodocus specimen had been found in the Morrison Formation of the western United States.

Sergio Sánchez Fenollosa, PhD student in biodiversity and evolutionary biology at Fundación Dinópolis and lead author of the study, explains: "We are delighted with this discovery.

"It was an exciting and continuous process of seeing the pieces of the puzzle gradually fall into place. From the early stages of the osteological study, we noticed strong similarities with several diplodocine sauropods. As we looked more closely at the anatomy, we began to identify a combination of features characteristic of Diplodocus species. Then, as we carried out different evolutionary analyses, they kept pointing in the same direction. With each new result, the picture became clearer: we were looking at a Diplodocus."

Sergio adds: "And what is more, the outcome of the dig is some of the strongest paleontological evidence for episodes of dispersal and faunal exchange between the two continents across the proto-Atlantic Ocean during the Late Jurassic.

"Essentially, this discovery allows us to better understand Iberian Mesozoic ecosystems and the diversity of sauropod dinosaurs that inhabited the European Jurassic."

A Jurassic Connection Between Continents

The Spanish Diplodocus lived roughly 150 million years ago, near the end of the Jurassic Period. Its presence in Europe provides strong evidence that dinosaurs were able to move between North America and Europe during this time.

Researchers believe these animals may have crossed temporary land bridges that appeared when sea levels fell during regressive phases of the proto-North Atlantic Ocean.

The finding therefore offers more than a new location for Diplodocus. It also provides evidence of periods when dinosaur populations and other animals could move between the two continents.

A 25 Meter Giant in Spain

Co-author Dr Alberto Cobos, managing director of Fundación Dinópolis, points out: "The Diplodocus from El Castellar was approximately 25 meters long (comparable in size to its North American relatives), making it another of the giant sauropods of the Spanish Jurassic, alongside other sauropod dinosaurs from Teruel with characteristics very different from those of diplodocids, such as Turiasaurus and Losillasaurus, among others.

"The fossils of all these dinosaurs, including those of the new Diplodocus specimen, make Teruel a reference place for understanding this great diversity."

The newly identified Diplodocus therefore joins an already impressive collection of enormous sauropods known from the Spanish Jurassic. Together, these fossils reveal just how varied the giant dinosaurs living in the region once were.

Exceptionally Preserved Diplodocus Fossils

The excellent preservation of the specimen allowed the researchers to recognize several anatomical traits associated with Diplodocus, including:

Large pneumatic cavities inside the vertebrae

Deep longitudinal grooves along the underside of the tail bones

Distinctive forked chevron bones with unique medial fossae

Elongated vertebral centra without lateral ridges

The team combined traditional anatomical comparisons with advanced phylogenetic analyses (including maximum parsimony and Bayesian inference methods). Their results placed the specimen securely within the Diplodocus genus and identified it as a close relative of Diplodocus hallorum.

The fossils are now displayed for continued research and public education in the dinosaur hall of the Museo Aragonés de Paleontología at Dinópolis in Teruel, a city in eastern Spain located roughly between Madrid and Valencia.

One of the World's Most Famous Dinosaurs

Diplodocus ranks among the most recognizable dinosaurs ever discovered. It is known for its enormous length (up to 25 meters), long whip-like tail, and relatively small head.

Since Diplodocus was first discovered in the United States in 1878, casts of its skeleton have appeared in major natural history museums around the world, particularly during the early 20th century. Those displays helped turn Diplodocus into an international symbol of paleontology and one of the most familiar dinosaurs in popular culture.

Its frequent appearances in museum exhibitions and audiovisual productions about dinosaurs have also helped make it one of the best-known "terrible lizards" among the general public.

A Diverse Dinosaur Ecosystem in Jurassic Iberia

The discovery also adds new information about the remarkable dinosaur diversity of eastern Iberia during the Late Jurassic.

The area surrounding the fossil site has produced remains from numerous dinosaur groups, including sauropods, theropods, stegosaurs, and ornithopods. Together, these fossils suggest that the ancient coastal environments of the region supported complex and highly diverse dinosaur ecosystems.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of the first confirmed Diplodocus fossil outside North America represents a significant scientific breakthrough that broadens understanding of dinosaur distribution and Late Jurassic ecosystems. It has broad significance for paleontology and public education, with well-detailed context about the find, its implications for continental connections, and the diversity of dinosaurs in Europe.
articles.personality_title: First Diplodocus dinosaur found outside North America in Spain
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Diplodocus is a famous dinosaur known from North America, where its fossils have been found for over a century. Until now, no confirmed Diplodocus fossils had been discovered anywhere else in the world.

**What happened** – Scientists found a 150-million-year-old Diplodocus fossil in Spain, marking the first time this dinosaur has been identified outside North America. The fossil includes 14 well-preserved tail bones and other parts, allowing researchers to confirm it belongs to the Diplodocus family. The discovery was made at La Tejería site in Teruel, Spain, by a team from Fundación Dinópolis.

**Impact** – This find shows that Diplodocus and related dinosaurs lived in Europe too, which changes what scientists thought about how dinosaurs spread across continents. It suggests dinosaurs could travel between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic period, possibly using temporary land bridges when sea levels dropped. The fossil also adds to the known variety of giant dinosaurs that lived in ancient Spain.

**What's next step** – The fossil will be studied further and displayed at the Museo Aragonés de Paleontología in Teruel. Researchers will continue exploring how dinosaurs moved between continents and how diverse the ecosystems were in Jurassic Europe.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, a Diplodocus dinosaur has been found in Europe, revealing new connections between ancient continents and expanding our knowledge of dinosaur life in the Late Jurassic.
articles.personality_title_fr: Premier Diplodocus découvert en Europe, hors d'Amérique du Nord
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Diplodocus est un dinosaure célèbre connu uniquement en Amérique du Nord, où ses fossiles ont été découverts depuis plus d’un siècle. Jusqu’ici, aucun fossile confirmé de Diplodocus n’avait été trouvé ailleurs dans le monde.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont découvert un fossile de Diplodocus vieux de 150 millions d’années en Espagne, marquant la première identification de ce dinosaure en dehors de l’Amérique du Nord. Le fossile comprend 14 vertèbres de la queue bien conservées et d’autres os, permettant aux chercheurs de confirmer qu’il s’agit bien d’un Diplodocus. La découverte a eu lieu sur le site de La Tejería à Teruel, en Espagne, par une équipe de la Fundación Dinópolis.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que le Diplodocus et des dinosaures similaires vivaient aussi en Europe, ce qui change la compréhension des scientifiques sur la façon dont les dinosaures se sont répandus entre les continents. Elle suggère que les dinosaures pouvaient voyager entre l’Amérique du Nord et l’Europe à la fin du Jurassique, probablement via des ponts terrestres temporaires lors de baisses du niveau de la mer. Ce fossile enrichit aussi la diversité connue des grands dinosaures qui habitaient l’Espagne ancienne.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le fossile sera étudié plus en détail et exposé au Museo Aragonés de Paleontología à Teruel. Les chercheurs continueront à étudier comment les dinosaures circulaient entre les continents et la diversité des écosystèmes du Jurassique européen.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Pour la première fois, un Diplodocus a été trouvé en Europe, révélant de nouvelles connexions entre les continents anciens et élargissant nos connaissances sur la vie des dinosaures à la fin du Jurassique.
articles.personality_title_es: Primer Diplodocus descubierto en Europa fuera de Norteamérica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Diplodocus es un dinosaurio famoso conocido solo en Norteamérica, donde se han encontrado sus fósiles por más de un siglo. Hasta ahora, no se había confirmado ningún fósil de Diplodocus en otras partes del mundo.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos encontraron un fósil de Diplodocus de 150 millones de años en España, la primera vez que se identifica este dinosaurio fuera de Norteamérica. El fósil incluye 14 huesos de la cola bien conservados y otras partes, lo que permitió confirmar que pertenece a la familia Diplodocus. El hallazgo fue en el sitio La Tejería, en Teruel, España, por un equipo de la Fundación Dinópolis.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que Diplodocus y dinosaurios similares vivieron también en Europa, lo que cambia la idea que tenían los científicos sobre cómo se dispersaron los dinosaurios entre continentes. Sugiere que pudieron cruzar entre Norteamérica y Europa durante el Jurásico tardío, posiblemente usando puentes terrestres temporales cuando bajaba el nivel del mar. Además, el fósil amplía la variedad de dinosaurios gigantes conocidos en la antigua España.

**Próximos pasos** – El fósil será estudiado más y exhibido en el Museo Aragonés de Paleontología en Teruel. Los investigadores seguirán explorando cómo se movían los dinosaurios entre continentes y la diversidad de los ecosistemas jurásicos europeos.

**Resumen en una frase** – Por primera vez, un Diplodocus fue encontrado en Europa, mostrando nuevas conexiones entre continentes antiguos y ampliando nuestro conocimiento sobre la vida de los dinosaurios en el Jurásico tardío.
